Potential Aquaculture Locations within Exclusive Economic Zones

Analysis of surface sea temperature and bathymetry to find suitable locations for aquaculture based on species parameters.

Introduction

Aquaculture is a viable solution to help address over-fishing while providing ocean foods to communities that rely on them. It additionally creates a job sector increasing local employment opportunities. Though there are many factors in choosing suitable locations for aquaculture, sea surface temperature (SST) and bathymetry are two key considerations. This analysis focuses on creating a function that identifies potential aquaculture locations based on SST and bathymetry species requirements. Further, the findings of potential aquaculture locations for each species is broken into Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ).

Code 
# load in necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(tmap)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)

Read in data

EEZ data is available through marineregions.org. Since this is vector data we use the sf package to read in the data.

Code 
# read in eez data as an sf object
eez_sf <- read_sf(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations","data","wc_regions_clean.shp"))

Bathymetry data is available through the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO). Since this is raster data we use the terra package to read in the data. Note: The word depth is used throughout this analysis and refers to bathymetry.

Code 
# read in raster depth data
depth <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "depth.tif"))

SST data was acquired from the NOAA’s 5km Daily Global Satellite Sea Surface Temperature Anomaly v3.1. Since this is raster data we use the terra package to read in the data. SST data from 2008 to 2012 is used and averaged for this analysis. This averaging is necessary to account for year to year variations in SST.

We stack all of the SST data for each year to make a single raster.

Code 
# read in raster sea surface temperature data
sst_2008 <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "average_annual_sst_2008.tif"))
sst_2009 <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "average_annual_sst_2009.tif"))
sst_2010 <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "average_annual_sst_2010.tif"))
sst_2011 <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "average_annual_sst_2011.tif"))
sst_2012 <- rast(here::here("blog", "potential-aquaculture-locations", "data", "average_annual_sst_2012.tif"))

# stack data into a raster stack
sst <- c(sst_2008, sst_2009, sst_2010, sst_2011, sst_2012)
Code 
# remove unnecessary raster data
rm(sst_2008, sst_2009, sst_2010, sst_2011, sst_2012)

Check CRS

CRS is one of the three components that is essential to check before plotting. CRS must match for all of the data to accurately perform functions on different data.

To check the CRS of a raster use crs and to check the CRS of a simple feature object use st_crs.

Warning messages are especially useful as they’ll alert when the specification is not met.

Code 
  if (crs(sst)== crs(depth)){
  print("it's a match!")
}else {
    warning("still not a match")
}
Warning: still not a match

Since not all of the CRS match we need to change some of the CRS. Make all of the CRS match the SST CRS. From personal experience matching the CRS of raster data is less prone to causing errors down the road due to incorrect CRS.

Code 
depth <- project(depth, crs(sst))
eez_sf <- st_transform(eez_sf, crs(sst))

We use warning messages again to make sure the CRS alterations were successful. They were!

Code 
  if (crs(sst)== crs(depth)){
  print("it's a match!")
}else {
    warning("still not a match")
}
[1] "it's a match!"

Data processing

This analysis works based on the mean of Sea Surface Temperature (SST) measured between 2008 and 2012 so we use map algebra to calculate the mean. This analysis is also based on Celsius so we subtract 273 to convert all of the values from the Kelvin scale to the Celsius scale with a global operation.

Code 
# calculate the mean of sst 
mean_sst <- mean(sst)

# convert the units from kelvin to celsius
mean_sst <- mean_sst - 273

To reiterate, the three important aspects when working with spatial data is that the extent, resolution, and positions. For this analysis SST and depth need to have the same extent, resolution, and positions. Let’s crop to make sure the extent of the rasters are the same.

Code 
# crop the depth raster 
depth <- crop(depth, mean_sst)

Then we resample to make sure that the resolutions of the rasters are the same.

Code 
depth <- resample(depth, mean_sst)

Let’s add another warning message to make sure the extents and resolutions match for the SST and depth data frames.

Code 
  if (ext(mean_sst)== ext(depth)){
  print("extents match!")
}else {
    warning("extents not a match")
}
[1] "extents match!"
Code 
if (res(mean_sst)[1]== res(depth)[1] & res(mean_sst)[2]== res(depth)[2]){
   print("resolutions match!")
 }else {
     warning("resolutions not a match")
 }
[1] "resolutions match!"

Find cells where conditions are satisfied for both the SST and depth for specific species.

The steps to finding locations that satisfy conditions for a specific species based on SST and depth are: 1. Make a matrix 2. Reclassify based on that matrix

Sea surface temperature is adequate for oysters in the range of 11-30°C. Classify sea surface temperature to find those areas that are potential zones for oyster aquaculture.

We assign anything less than 11 degrees Celsius and anything more that 30 degrees Celsius to 0 since these areas are not suitable for oyster aquaculture. Anything between the range of 11 and 30 degrees Celsius we assign a 1 to signify these areas are suitable for oyster aquaculture.

Code 
# create a classification matrix for sst
sst_matrix <- matrix(c(-Inf, 11, 0, 
            11, 30, 1, 
            30, Inf, 0),
            ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# classify where suitable sst habitat for oysters are
sst_classified <- classify(mean_sst, rcl = sst_matrix)

Oysters can survive between the depths of 70 and 0 meters below the sea surface. Classify depth to find those areas that are potential zones for oyster aquaculture.

We assign anything below 70 meters and anything above sea level to 0 since these areas are not suitable for oyster aquaculture. Anything between the range of 70 meters deep and sea level we assign a 1 to signify these areas are suitable for oyster aquaculture.

Code 
# create a classification matrix for depth
depth_matrix = matrix(c(-Inf, -70, 0,
                  -70, 0, 1,
                  0, Inf, 0),
                  ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# classify where suitable depth habitat for oysters are
depth_classified <- classify(depth, rcl = depth_matrix)

Create a function to determine what locations are suited for oyster aquaculture based on both sea surface temperature and depth.

Anywhere a zero is present for either depth or SST will result in a 0 since anything times zero is zero. Only areas where there is a one for both depth and SST will be left.

Code 
suitable_habitat <- function(rast1, rast2){

  rast1 * rast2
}

Apply the function to determine what areas that are suitable based on both SST and depth for oyster aquaculture. Then we set anything that is a zero to NA to avoid any analysis issues moving forward.

Code 
suit_oyster_aqu <- lapp(c(sst_classified, depth_classified), fun = suitable_habitat)

# set any locations with a zero to NA
suit_oyster_aqu[suit_oyster_aqu == 0] <- NA

Here are some preliminary maps to assess differences between suitable locations based on depth, SST, and both depth and SST.

Intermediate mapping allows us to see if what we think we are doing is what we’re doing in reality.

Code 
# suitable depth for oyster aquaculture
tm_basemap("Esri.OceanBasemap") +
tm_shape(sst_classified) +
  tm_raster(style = "cat",
            palette = c("skyblue", "red"),
            labels = c("unsuitable", "suitable"),
            title = "Sea Surface Temperature (SST)") + 
  tm_title(text = "Suitable SST for Oyster Aquaculture",
           size = 12) +
  tm_compass() +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_layout(fontsize = 2,
            scale = 0.5,
            compass.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
            scalebar.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
            ) +
   tm_layout(component.autoscale = FALSE)
Code 
# suitable depth for oyster aquaculture
tm_shape(depth_classified) +
  tm_raster(style = "cat",
            palette = c("skyblue", "red"),
            labels = c("unsuitable", "suitable"),
            title = "Depth suitability") + 
  tm_title(text = "Suitable Depths for Oyster Aquaculture",
           size = 12) + 
  tm_compass() +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_layout(fontsize = 2,
            scale = 0.5,
            compass.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
            scalebar.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
            ) +
   tm_layout(component.autoscale = FALSE)
Code 
# suitable locations for oyster aquaculture
tm_basemap("Esri.OceanBasemap") +
tm_shape(suit_oyster_aqu) +
  tm_raster(style = "cat",
            palette = c( "red"),
            labels = c("suitable area"),
            title = "Aquaculture suitability") + 
  tm_title(text = "Suitable Oyster Aquaculture Locations",
           size = 12) +
  tm_title("Based on depth and SST", size=12) +
  tm_compass() +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_layout(fontsize = 2,
            scale = 0.5,
            compass.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
            scalebar.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
            ) +
   tm_layout(component.autoscale = FALSE)

How much suitable aquaculture space is there in each Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)?

Find the suitable aquaculture locations for each EEZ.

We rasterize the vetor data so that the operations can be applied smoothly between the two objects. Since we’re only interested in the suitable habitat within the Exclusive Economic Zones so we crop the suitable oyster aquaculture zones by the EEZ object.

We’re then interested in the size of the cells that are quitable in each EEZ area so we use the zonal function to calculate the suitable areas.

Code 
# rasterize the eez sf object
eez_rast <- rasterize(eez_sf, suit_oyster_aqu, field = "rgn_id")

# select only suitable oyster aquaculture locations that are within the eez
eez_oysters <- mask(suit_oyster_aqu, eez_sf)

# calculate average size of cells
avg_area <- cellSize(eez_oysters, unit = "km")

# sum the suitable aquaculture locations based on eez zones
oyst_area <- zonal(x = (eez_oysters * avg_area), 
                   z = eez_rast, 
                   fun = "sum", 
                   na.rm = TRUE) |> 
  as.data.frame()

# join to make one data frame with the total area
eez_sf <-  left_join(eez_sf, oyst_area, by = "rgn_id")

# rename new column 
eez_sf <- eez_sf |> 
  rename("area" = "lyr1")

How much suitable space is there for oyster aquaculture?

We can see the amount of area that is suitable throughout the West Coast. This is an interesting metric for any stakeholders who might be interested in seeing whether oyster aquaculture is something to pursue.

Code 
total_oyst <- sum(eez_sf$area)

The total amount of space in the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ) on the West Coast that are suitable for oyster aquaculture based on suitable sea surface temperature and suitable bathymetry is 1.1799613^{4} km^2.

Here’s a final map with the coloration of the EEZ zones signifying the total suiatable aquaculture area that each zone contains.

Code 
tm_basemap("Esri.OceanBasemap") +
tm_shape(eez_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = 'area',
              breaks = c(400, 1000, 1500, 3000, 3400, 4000),
              palette = c("#EEF5FC",
                          "#96C3ED",
                          "#237DD1",
                          "#1B5E9D",
                          "#0C3259"),
              title = "Suitable Aquaculture Area (km^2)") +
  tm_text("rgn", size = 0.7) +
  tm_shape(eez_oysters) + 
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_categorical(labels = (c("Suitable Areas", "Unsuitable")),
                                          values= (c("red", "white"))),
            col.legend = tm_legend("Aquaculture Areas")) + 
  tm_compass() +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_title("Suitable Oyster Aquaculture Area in Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ)",
           size = 3) +
  tm_layout(fontsize = 2,
            scale = 0.5,
            compass.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
            scalebar.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))

We also make a polished table to visualize the differences in suitable aquaculture area and verify the map above is accurate.

Code

  st_drop_geometry() |> 
  rename("State" = "rgn",
         "Suitable area (km^2)" = "area")

# create a table with the counts of adequate aquaculture zones
eez_kable |>
  select("State", "Suitable area (km^2)") |>
  kbl(caption = "Suitable Oyster Aquaculture areas on the West Coast based on Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ).") |>

Potential aquaculture locations for different species

We can combine all the steps we conducted above to make a function that can work on calculating potential aquaculture areas for any species. We replace variables that would vary for different species in a by making those arguments in a function. Function arguments should also include all of the necessary data frames for clarity. In the potent_aqu function we need to use three data frames. The SST, EEZ, and depth data frames. Additionally, we need to change the minimum and maximum values for the suitable SST and depth of each species. Species name is also an argument for clarity and to add the name to the title of the plot.

Code 
potent_aqu <- function (sst, 
                        eez_sf, 
                        depth, 
                        min_sst, 
                        max_sst, 
                        min_depth, 
                        max_depth, 
                        species_name){

# make all of the CRS match
depth <- project(depth, crs(sst))
st_crs(eez_sf) <- crs(sst)

# calculate the mean of sst 
mean_sst <- mean(sst)
# convert the units from kelvin to celcius
mean_sst <- mean_sst - 273 

# crop the depth raster to match the sst extent
depth <- crop(depth, mean_sst)

# resample depth raster to match the sst resolution
depth <- resample(depth, mean_sst)

# create a classification matrix for sst
sst_matrix <- matrix(c(-Inf, min_sst, 0, 
            min_sst, max_sst, 1, 
            max_sst, Inf, 0),
            ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# classify where suitable sst habitat for oysters are
sst_classified <- classify(mean_sst, rcl = sst_matrix)

# create a classification matrix for depth
depth_matrix = matrix(c(-Inf, min_depth, 0,
                  min_depth, max_depth, 1,
                  max_depth, Inf, 0),
                  ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)

# classify where suitable depth habitat for oysters are
depth_classified <- classify(depth, rcl = depth_matrix)

# function to determine what habitats are suitable 
suitable_habitat <- function(rast1, rast2){

  rast1 * rast2
}

# find suitable locations for aquaculture
suit_aqu <- lapp(c(sst_classified, depth_classified), fun = suitable_habitat)

# rasterize the eez sf object
eez_rast <- rasterize(eez_sf, suit_aqu, field = "rgn_id")

# set any locations with a zero to NA
suit_aqu[suit_aqu == 0] <- NA

# select only suitable oyster aquaculture locations that are within the eez
eez_spec <- mask(suit_aqu, eez_sf)

# calculate average size of cells
avg_area <- cellSize(eez_spec, unit = "km")

# sum the suitable aquaculture locations based on eez zones
spec_area <- zonal(x = (eez_spec * avg_area), 
                   z = eez_rast, 
                   fun = "sum", 
                   na.rm = TRUE) |> 
              as.data.frame()

# join to make one data frame with the total area
spec_area_eez <-  left_join(eez_sf, spec_area, by = "rgn_id")

# rename new column 
spec_area_eez <- spec_area_eez |> 
  rename("spec_area" = "lyr1")

# map the eez's based on the amount of suitable area per region
tm_basemap("Esri.OceanBasemap") +
tm_shape(spec_area_eez) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "spec_area",
              fill.legend = tm_legend("Suitable Aquaculture Area (km^2)")) +
  tm_text("rgn", size = 0.7) +
  tm_shape(eez_oysters) + 
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_categorical(labels = (c("Suitable Areas", "Unsuitable")),
                                          values= (c("red", "white"))),
            col.legend = tm_legend("Aquaculture Areas")) + 
  tm_compass() +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_title( paste("Suitable Aquaculture Area in Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZ): ", species_name), 
           size = 2) +
  tm_layout(fontsize = 2,
            scale = 0.5,
            compass.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"),
            scalebar.position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
            ) 
}

Additional species of interest: Red Sea Urchin, Mesocentrotus franciscanus

Let’s try out our function!

Sea surface temperature is adequate for red sea urchins in the range of 6.75-13.02°C. Red sea urchins can survive between the depths of 125 and 0 meters below the sea surface.

Code 
# run the function to identify potential suitable areas for red sea urchin aquaculture 
potent_aqu(sst, eez_sf, depth, 6.75, 13.02, -125, 0, "Mesocentrotus franciscanus")

Reflection

Analyzing potential aquaculture locations based on SST and bathymetry is only the first step in finding suitable locations for new aquaculture endeavors. One limitation of the above analysis is that SST is an average taken from 2008 to 2012. With climate change shifting temperatures, projection data would be important to include in analyzing best future aquaculture sites. Referencing species native ranges is also essential to reducing any potential negative outcomes of introducing non-native species.
